subsection: 12. Youth and popular culture (including sport) and the mass media

notes.b: John Lennon was a founding member of The Beatles, the band that turned British pop into a worldwide phenomenon and made its members the first global pop stars (mass-audience performers made famous by records, television and press coverage).
points: Lennon was born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940. He formed the Quarrymen in 1957, and the group later became The Beatles (the name was adopted in 1960) with Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, who joined in 1962.
The Beatles played long residencies in Hamburg from 1960 to 1962 and at the Cavern Club in Liverpool, which gave them years of live experience before they were nationally famous.
Brian Epstein became their manager in 1962 and polished their image, while George Martin produced their records. Their first UK number one, From Me to You, came in 1963.

The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964 put them on American television and gave them a mass audience in the USA, the start of the 'British invasion' of American pop. Beatlemania, the screaming crowds and saturation press coverage that followed the band, spread across Western Europe.

Lennon and McCartney wrote most of the Beatles' songs. Albums such as Rubber Soul (1965) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) showed that pop music could be an art form and not just disposable entertainment.

In June 1967 the Beatles performed All You Need Is Love on Our World, the first live global television broadcast by satellite, which was watched by hundreds of millions of people. This shows how television and pop music together created a worldwide audience.
In 1966 Lennon remarked that the Beatles were more popular than Jesus. This provoked protests and record burnings in parts of the USA, and it showed the controversy his fame attracted.

Epstein died in August 1967, which weakened the group, and the Beatles broke up in 1970. Disputes about business and music contributed to the split, so Epstein's death was one cause and not the only one.
notes.tip: For a short Lennon answer, give four to six dated points in order: birth date and city, the Quarrymen and the Beatles, Hamburg and the Cavern Club, the Ed Sullivan Show, songwriting with McCartney. Don't confuse the Ed Sullivan Show (February 1964) with Our World (June 1967).

notes.h: Key personality: John Lennon as peace campaigner, solo artist and victim of 1980
notes.b: After the Beatles became world famous, Lennon used that fame for the anti-war cause. His protests and his solo career brought him both admirers and enemies, and his life ended violently in 1980.
points: In March 1969 he and Yoko Ono held a 'bed-in' at the Amsterdam Hilton to promote peace. His song Give Peace a Chance (1969) became an anthem of the anti-war movement.
He returned his MBE (a British honour) in November 1969 in protest at British support for the US in Vietnam and the Nigerian civil war, a gesture that made his protest a public act.
He and Yoko Ono ran peace campaigns including the War Is Over billboard campaign of December 1969, which used advertising-style posters to spread an anti-war message.
His solo career produced the Plastic Ono Band records and Imagine (1971), a song that is judged both radical and commercially successful.
The US authorities tried to deport him from 1972 because of his anti-war activity. He won the right to stay, and he was granted a green card (permanent residence) in 1976.
From 1975 he spent five years as a househusband caring for his son Sean, who was born in 1975, before returning to music with the album Double Fantasy (1980).
He was shot dead outside his home in New York on 8 December 1980, and his death was widely mourned across Europe and America.
notes.tip: Keep the three 1969 events apart: the Amsterdam bed-in in March, the return of the MBE in November and the War Is Over billboards in December. Examiners credit dated statements, and the bed-in and Imagine are central to the peace message.

notes.h: Key personality: John Lennon in the eyes of contemporaries and historians
notes.b: Lennon divided opinion in his lifetime, and historians still weigh his importance. Examiners on the Higher paper reward a judgement on impact, controversy and legacy.
points: Contemporaries saw him as a symbol of youthful rebellion: to fans he was an idol and a hero of the peace movement, while to critics such as those who burned Beatles records he was a danger to morals.
The American authorities treated him as a political danger, which is why they tried to deport him in 1972 because of his anti-war activity.
Historians present him as a symbol of the 1960s counterculture, meaning a culture that rejected the dominant values of society, and they treat the Beatles as the first global pop stars.
The Beatles are also seen as the model for later artists who wrote their own songs, because Lennon and McCartney showed that a group could write as well as perform its material.
Historians judge his post-Beatles work as both radical and commercially successful, and critics note that his radicalism was sometimes self-contradictory.
notes.tip: On the Higher paper Lennon appears as one of several personalities. Aim for impact (global pop star, peace message), controversy (the 1966 remark, the deportation attempt) and the views of historians, and explain why he was a symbol of youth culture.

notes.h: The teenager and the rise of youth culture
notes.b: After 1945 young people became a distinct group in society with money, music and style of their own. This happened because of post-war prosperity, more schooling and new media that were aimed at them.
points: The word teenager (a young person treated as a distinct group with its own spending power and culture) was in common use in the USA from the 1940s, and the idea spread to Europe from there.

Post-war recovery and the 'economic miracle' brought rising wages and full employment in Western Europe in the 1950s and 1960s, so young people had more spending money for records, clothes and cinema.

The baby boom after 1945 and the expansion of secondary and university education kept young people in school longer and put more of them together with others their own age. This gave them a shared identity, which helped to fuel youth rebellion.

The Cold War division of Europe shaped what young people could hear, wear and watch. In the West they were free to follow American and British trends, while in the East the authorities tried to restrict them.
The 45 rpm single, introduced by RCA in the USA in 1949, made records cheap enough for teenagers to buy with their own money.
Radio Luxembourg, funded by advertising, broadcast pop music in English to Britain and Europe, so teenagers could hear music that official stations did not play.
Teenage magazines and dances created a youth media and a social scene of their own, so young people became a market that businesses competed to serve.
notes.tip: Essays often ask how far youth became a distinct group. Define the teenager first, then explain spending power, schooling and media as causes, with a named example for each.

notes.h: Rock 'n' roll, American influence and Live Aid
notes.b: Rock 'n' roll came from America and reached Europe in the mid-1950s. It alarmed many adults, and later pop events showed how youth culture could be used for a cause.
points: The USA's cultural influence on Europe after 1945 reached young people through films, music, jeans and consumer goods, which made American style attractive.
Rock 'n' roll arrived in Europe in the mid-1950s. Bill Haley's Rock Around the Clock reached the UK singles chart in 1955, and Elvis Presley's first UK hits came in 1956.
Films about rebellious youth, The Wild One (1953) and Rebel Without a Cause (1955), made rebellion look glamorous to teenagers.
Many adults feared that rock 'n' roll and these films encouraged delinquency (youthful law-breaking), so critics saw the music as a threat to order and morals.

Live Aid, organised by the Irish singer Bob Geldof, was held at Wembley in London and in Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 to raise money for famine relief in Ethiopia. A very large global television audience watched, so it was a late example of youth culture used for a cause.
notes.tip: Back up any claim about youth rebellion with a named group, date or event, for example Bill Haley in 1955 or Live Aid in 1985. Examiners deduct marks for unsupported generalisation such as 'youth rebelled'.

notes.h: Fashion and subcultures in the 1950s and 1960s
notes.b: Dress and music were how young people marked themselves out from their elders. A subculture is a youth group with its own style, music and values, and several of them sparked public debate.
points: Teddy boys in 1950s Britain wore Edwardian-style jackets and became associated with delinquency, so their critics treated them as proof that rock 'n' roll was a threat.
The Mods and Rockers of Britain clashed at English seaside resorts in 1964, beginning at Clacton at Easter and followed by Margate and Brighton at Whitsun (May 1964).
The press coverage of these clashes exaggerated them and created a 'moral panic', a wave of public alarm about youth out of proportion to the events.
Fashion expressed the new youth market. Mary Quant of London helped to make the miniskirt famous in the 1960s, and Carnaby Street in London became a centre of fashion.
Hippies of the late 1960s adopted long hair, flowers and communal living. They were part of the counterculture, which rejected the dominant values of society.
notes.tip: Don't give one date for all the seaside clashes of 1964. Name 1964 and say the press helped to create the moral panic. Keep teddy boys (1950s), Mods and Rockers (1960s) and punks (1970s) distinct.

notes.h: Jeans, punk and later youth styles
notes.b: Youth style was also political and national. Jeans carried a message about America and freedom, and later styles expressed the anger of a generation hit by economic hardship.
points: Jeans symbolised America and freedom. They were worn by young people across Europe and highly valued in the East, where they were scarce.
Punk arose in 1976–77 with the Sex Pistols and The Clash. It expressed the anger of unemployed young people in the recession.
The Sex Pistols' God Save the Queen was released on 27 May 1977, about ten days before the Silver Jubilee bank holiday on 7 June. It was in the charts during Jubilee week, when it reached number 2.

Skinheads and later the new romantics, mostly in Britain, were other styles that fused fashion, music and class identity. They show that each generation's subculture reflected its own social conditions.
notes.tip: Link each subculture to its cause, for example punk to unemployment and recession, and don't treat all European youth alike.

notes.h: 1968: causes and the events in Paris
notes.b: In 1968 student protest turned into a political crisis in France. It combined anger about universities with wider hostility to authority.
points: The causes were overcrowded universities with strict rules, opposition to the Vietnam War, hostility to authority and distrust of consumer society.
Student protests began at Nanterre, a university on the edge of Paris, in March 1968 as a demand for university reform and a protest against restrictions there.
In May 1968 the protests moved to the Sorbonne, the centre of the protests in Paris.
The 'Night of the Barricades' of 10–11 May 1968 saw fighting between students and police in the Latin Quarter of Paris.

The protests widened into attacks on de Gaulle's government and on consumer society, and they spread into a general strike involving millions of workers in France, which brought the country close to a standstill.
notes.tip: Don't merge the Paris protests with the Prague Spring: they were different in cause. Remember Nanterre as the start and the Sorbonne as the centre.

notes.h: 1968: de Gaulle's response, other countries and results
notes.b: The French government survived 1968, but the protests spread across Europe and changed attitudes more than they changed governments.
points: Charles de Gaulle, the French president, left Paris briefly on 29 May 1968. His supporters then won a large majority in the June 1968 election, and he resigned in April 1969 after losing a referendum.
Students in West Germany, led by figures such as Rudi Dutschke, protested against the Vietnam War and the legacy of the Nazi past.
In Czechoslovakia students supported the Prague Spring, and in Poland student protests in March 1968 were suppressed. Unrest also hit Italy, Britain and Spain.
The 1968 protests did not overthrow governments, but they changed attitudes to authority, sexuality and the role of universities.
The 1968 movement influenced the women's, environmental and peace movements of the 1970s.
notes.tip: Examiners expect the judgement that attitudes changed more than governments. Give causes, the Paris events, de Gaulle's response and the outcome in order, with dates.

notes.h: Football and the money of sport
notes.b: Football grew from a local game into a Europe-wide spectacle in the 1950s and 1960s. Television and money turned players into celebrities.
points: The European Champion Clubs' Cup began in the 1955–56 season and became the leading club competition in Western Europe. Real Madrid won the first five European Cups, from 1956 to 1960.
West Germany beat Hungary in the final of the 1954 World Cup, the 'Miracle of Bern'. The win was a boost to national morale.
England won the World Cup at Wembley on 30 July 1966, and the BBC's television coverage made the tournament a mass event across Europe.
Television transformed football, and money flowed in through broadcasting rights, sponsorship and advertising.
This money made stars such as Johan Cruyff and George Best celebrities across Europe. Pelé is a global example, not a European one, because he was Brazilian.
notes.tip: Sport questions reward links to television and money, not a list of results. Don't confuse the European Cup (club football, from 1955–56) with the World Cup (national teams).

notes.h: The Olympics and the Cold War
notes.b: In the Cold War the Olympic Games became a contest between rival political systems, and the medal table was used to measure which one was winning. Politics and violence also intruded on the Games.
points: The Soviet Union entered the Olympic Games for the first time at Helsinki in 1952 and made the medal table a measure of the rival systems.
East Germany, with a population of about 17 million, finished near the top in the 1970s and 1980s. East Germany also ran a state-sponsored doping programme, which was exposed after 1990.
At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics the Hungary–USSR water polo match, played weeks after the Soviet invasion of Hungary, was known as the 'blood in the water' match.
The 1972 Munich Olympics were marred by the killing of eleven Israeli athletes and coaches by Palestinian militants (Black September) on 5–6 September 1972.
The United States and some of its allies boycotted the Moscow Olympics of 1980 after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
The Soviet Union and most of its allies boycotted the Los Angeles Olympics of 1984, a response that mirrored the 1980 boycott.
notes.tip: Sport questions reward Cold War links: the Olympics, the boycotts, East German success and Munich. Keep Moscow 1980 (Western boycott) apart from Los Angeles 1984 (Soviet-led boycott) and Munich 1972 (the attack) apart from Melbourne 1956 (water polo).

notes.b: Television was the most powerful new mass medium (a means of reaching large audiences, along with radio, cinema and the press). It changed how people received news, entertainment and advertising, and countries organised it in different ways.
points: Television spread from a few sets in 1950 to being owned by most West European households by the 1970s. The Coronation of Elizabeth II on 2 June 1953 persuaded many British families to buy a set.
Public broadcasting is funded by licence fees or the state and bound by public-service duties. The BBC in Britain, RAI in Italy and ARD (founded 1950) and ZDF (1963) in West Germany were examples.
The BBC, funded by the licence fee, was bound to inform, educate and entertain.
Commercial broadcasting is funded by advertising. ITV began in Britain in September 1955 and ended the BBC's monopoly of television.

Radio Luxembourg also depended on advertising, and the pirate radio ship Radio Caroline began broadcasting in 1964. Pirate radio was unlicensed, so it was not the same as ITV, and it played pop music the BBC did not provide.
Television changed advertising, news, politics and sport, and political leaders increasingly had to present themselves on screen.
notes.tip: For television questions give cause (technology, rising incomes), effect (advertising, politics, sport) and the public versus commercial contrast with named examples: BBC, ITV and Radio Luxembourg.

notes.h: Eurovision, the press and state control of the media
notes.b: Broadcasting crossed borders in Western Europe, but governments in some countries held tight control over it. The press also remained a powerful mass medium.
points: The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), founded in 1950, ran Eurovision, a network that linked national broadcasters and carried live coverage of major sporting events across borders.
The first Eurovision Song Contest was held in May 1956 at Lugano in Switzerland, and it became a shared event across Western Europe in the 1960s.
Newspapers remained influential. Mass-circulation tabloids such as Bild in West Germany and the Daily Mirror in Britain reached millions of readers.
In Italy and France the governments used state control of television, so broadcasting there was not independent of politics.
In the East the party used television for propaganda, though East Germans could often receive West German broadcasts.
notes.tip: Keep Eurovision (the cross-border network, with the Song Contest from 1956) distinct from the commercial channels. Name examples: Eurovision, Bild and the Daily Mirror.

notes.b: In the communist East, youth culture was shaped by official control and by Western music that slipped across the Iron Curtain. The authorities tried to manage it, and sometimes it turned into political dissent.
points: Young people in the East listened to Western music on Radio Luxembourg, Radio Free Europe and tapes copied by hand, and the authorities in the bloc tried to control rock music.
In Czechoslovakia the arrest and trial of members of the rock band the Plastic People of the Universe in 1976 helped to inspire Charter 77, so a case about music became a political protest.
In East Germany the state sponsored the Free German Youth (FDJ). A ban on Western beat music in 1965 was followed by a limited tolerance in the 1970s.
In the Soviet Union the Komsomol organised youth, and the stilyagi of the 1950s were young people who copied Western fashions and jazz.
notes.tip: Strong essays separate West from East. Marks are lost for treating all of Europe alike, so use the East's controlled version of youth culture as a contrast.

notes.b: Historians debate whether youth culture and the mass media were a form of liberation or a commercial system that absorbed rebellion. A good answer weighs both sides with dated evidence.
points: Achievements: youth culture broadened tastes and challenged the authority of schools, churches and parents, and it gave young people a voice in politics and art, as the 1968 protests showed.
Achievements: the mass media, from the Beatles to Eurovision and the World Cup, helped to create a shared European culture.
Limits: much youth culture was commercially packaged, and the record companies and advertisers shaped what young people bought.
Limits: the effects varied by class, country and gender, and in the East the version of youth culture on offer was controlled by the state.
Contemporaries saw youth culture as a moral danger, with newspapers and politicians warning about delinquency, while young people saw it as freedom.
Later historians see the period as a major turning point in the cultural life of Western Europe, but they stress that its effects were uneven.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher essay asks you to assess the impact of youth and popular culture, sport and the mass media on European society, 1945–1992. Give a clear thesis, balance achievements and limits, use specific dated evidence (the teenager, rock 'n' roll, the Beatles, 1968, television), and compare liberation with commercial manipulation.

keyTerms.definition: A young person between the ages of thirteen and nineteen, treated after the 1940s as a distinct group with its own spending power and culture.
A performer of popular music whose fame is spread through records, television and media coverage to a mass audience.
The means of communication, such as television, radio, cinema and the press, that reach large audiences.
A culture that rejects the dominant values of a society, as the youth movements of the 1960s did.
The mass enthusiasm for The Beatles in the early 1960s, marked by crowds and media attention.
Broadcasting funded by licence fees or the state and governed by public-service duties, as the BBC was.
A youth group with its own style, music and values, such as teddy boys, mods, rockers, hippies and punks.
The network of European television broadcasters, and its annual Song Contest, which began in 1956.
Radio or television funded by advertising, such as ITV in Britain, as opposed to public service broadcasting funded by the licence fee.
